rationale: A wins because it keeps the sharpest story alive without pretending the missing evidence exists: "The refusal to split cuts from unfilled roles is part of the story, not a footnote." B has good bones, but it commits a headline-level factual faceplant with "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes," which the update does not say. In PR strategy, that difference matters: A makes the founder answer the hard question before pitching; B occasionally writes the answer for them.
gaps_in_A: "When a Klarna customer disputes a charge, a chatbot may be the first one to rule on it" goes a half-step past the facts. The update says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes; it does not establish that the bot rules on disputes.
"Klarna is taking an AI-shrunk cost base to the public markets" is a useful markets frame, but "AI-shrunk cost base" implies causation and margin evidence the update does not yet prove.
The repeated "Decay: week" labels are too tidy. The IPO and consumer-protection stories may live on filing or regulator cadence, not the announcement clock.
gaps_in_B: "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" is invented. The update gives a general resolution-time figure and says advocates worry about disputes; it does not say AI resolves disputes, let alone in under two minutes.
"one of the only companies publishing operational numbers" is an unsupported comparative. Rare may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts.
"let attrition cut head count 20%" misstates the update. The fact is headcount fell about 20% partly through attrition, while Klarna will not split cuts from unfilled roles.

The data angle and labor angle chase the same reporter family: "AI-and-work or labor-economics desk" and "future-of-work or labor reporter." That overlap leaves the cleaner contact-center benchmark story on the floor.
